title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples

epigraph.quote: A component supplier's real moat is visible only when you trace the exact part on the shop floor, the tolerance it must hold, and the cost of failure to the customer.
epigraph.author: Manufacturing Underwriting Principle

web_blocks.html: Kross Limited runs two core product lines from its Jamshedpur forging, heat-treatment, and machining plants [2][6]. The first is Trailer Axles & Suspension Assemblies, and the second is Forged & Precision-Machined Components for M&HCVs and tractors [2][6]. In statutory filings, Kross reports as one auto-parts segment [3][4]. However, management data for FY24–H1 FY27 show a clear shift toward trailer systems, which now bring nearly half of total sales [3][4].

web_blocks.takeaway: Trailer axles and suspensions scaled from ~30%–33% of revenue post-COVID to 49% in Q2 FY27, turning Kross from a pure sub-component vendor into a system-level trailer running-gear supplier.

web_blocks.text: Segment 1: Trailer Axles & Suspension Assemblies — Concrete End-to-End Walkthrough

web_blocks.html: A heavy semi-trailer hauls 35 to 55 tonnes of steel coils, cement, or containers over rough Indian roads. Unlike a truck's driven rear axle, a trailer axle is a non-driven load beam. It must take vertical shock, braking torque, and cornering stress without cracking at the spindle weld. In the past, Indian trailer builders welded four steel plates into a square box or bought imported round axles [22].

Real-World Customer Example (Organized Trailer OEM / Fleet Builder): Picture a trailer maker like Tata International DLT or a regional builder making a 40-foot flatbed for steel coils. Their main pain point is weld fatigue. Multi-piece welded square beams crack along weld seams on overloaded roads, causing breakdowns and warranty claims. Kross fixes this with a pre-built 13-tonne or 16-tonne tri-axle kit based on a single-piece extruded seamless round axle beam [9][14]. On the Jamshedpur floor, Kross hot-extrudes a steel tube and upsets both ends into spindles without butt-welds [2][5]. It then induction-hardens the bearing seats and fits forged hubs, S-cam brake drums, ABS tone rings, and leaf-spring or air hangers [2][5]. The full kit ships as a bolt-on unit. Prices are set per axle-and-suspension kit with alloy steel pass-through terms, lifting revenue per trailer far above loose forgings.

To win more of the trailer bill of materials, Kross added hydraulic tipping jacks in FY26–FY27 for mining and road-building tippers [3][9]. Selling the axle, suspension, and tipping jack to the same builder lifts sales per vehicle with no extra sales team. Fleet owners also get one warranty across the whole undercarriage.

web_blocks.text: Segment 2: Forged & Precision-Machined M&HCV Components — Concrete End-to-End Walkthrough

web_blocks.html: Before Kross made trailer axles, it built its name on truck drivetrain and chassis forgings [1][13]. These parts sit inside the powertrain and suspension, where micron-level errors or metal failure stop the truck at once.

Real-World Customer Example (Ashok Leyland / Tata Motors Heavy Truck Line): Ashok Leyland named Kross a 'Super 8 Supplier' [4][13]. When an OEM builds a 35-tonne rigid truck, its rear differential must carry high torque up steep mine ramps [4][13]. Kross makes the rear axle shaft and companion flange for that driveline. In Jamshedpur, workers shear alloy steel bars, forge them in closed dies, CNC-turn them, roll the splines, and deep-harden the outer skin over a tough core [1][2]. Every batch passes ultrasonic and magnetic-particle crack checks in-house before just-in-time delivery [2]. OEM rate contracts reset every three to six months with steel indexation, yielding 12%–14% operating margins in normal years [1][7].

Beyond shafts and flanges, Kross makes anti-roll bars, stabilizer bars, differential spiders, bevel gears, and planet carriers for M&HCVs [1][6]. Each OEM platform uses unique spline shapes and heat-treat depths. Kross's in-house tool-and-die team cuts part-launch lead times, making OEM buyers slow to switch to untested rivals.

web_blocks.text: Segment 3: Agricultural Tractor & Off-Highway Components — Concrete End-to-End Walkthrough

web_blocks.html: Tractor parts make up about 12%–15% of total sales [3][13]. They give Kross a local demand cushion when highway truck freight slows [3][13]. Tractors work in mud, dust, and heavy field shocks, so they need tough forged linkages and power shafts.

Real-World Customer Example (Domestic Tractor OEM — TAFE / Sonalika): When a 50-HP farm tractor pulls a rotavator or heavy plough, engine power runs through the power take-off (PTO) shaft and rear hydraulic lift rockshaft [1][6]. Kross supplies forged PTO shafts, front axle spindles, and lift arms to tractor OEMs like TAFE and International Tractors [4][13]. It forges the blanks in-house, machines splines on CNC cells, and heat-treats parts to resist twisting loads. Kross is also testing forged prop-shaft and driveline parts for European Tier-1 buyers. Exports sit near ~8% of the parts business, and management aims for 40%–45% yearly export growth [9].

book_paragraphs: If you walked onto Kross Limited's Gamharia campus in Jamshedpur, you would not see consumer brands or software dashboards. You would hear the thud of closed-die forging hammers, smell quenching oil from induction-hardening lines, and see rows of CNC lathes turning heavy alloy steel. To evaluate this business properly, you and I need to break down its two major revenue engines—and trace a real part through each one.

The first engine, and the one driving growth since 2019, is Trailer Axles and Suspension Assemblies, which now accounts for 43% to 49% of total revenue. Think about what happens when a 40-foot semi-trailer carries 45 tonnes of steel coils over broken highway expansion joints. A trailer axle is not a powered gearset; it is a structural beam carrying immense bending loads. For years, Indian trailer builders welded four steel plates into a square box beam or bought expensive imports. Those welded seams are notorious failure points under overloaded road conditions. Kross solved this by commissioning India's first single-piece axle beam extrusion plant, where roughly 80% of its trailer axles are now formed as seamless, continuous beams without center-body welds. Sold as complete 13-tonne or 16-tonne axle-and-suspension kits—complete with hubs, brake drums, ABS rings, and newly added hydraulic tipping jacks—this segment turns Kross into a system supplier for trailer builders like Tata International DLT.

The second engine is Kross's legacy core: Forged and Precision-Machined Components for heavy trucks and tractors, representing the remaining 51% to 57% of revenue. Inside a heavy truck built by Ashok Leyland or Tata Motors, Kross makes the rear axle shafts, companion flanges, differential spiders, bevel gears, and anti-roll bars that transfer engine torque to the road. Imagine a 35-tonne tipper truck climbing out of an iron-ore mine in Odisha: every clutch drop sends a shockwave down the rear axle shaft. Kross shears alloy steel bars, upset-forgings them in closed dies, CNC-turns the profile, rolls the splines, and induction-hardens the outer skin before running ultrasonic crack checks. On the farm side—roughly 12% to 15% of the business—Kross supplies PTO shafts, front spindles, and hydraulic lift linkages to tractor makers such as TAFE and Sonalika, giving the top line a partial rural buffer when truck freight pauses.

Beyond domestic OEMs, Kross is also pushing into European Tier-1 driveline exports, currently about 8% of its component business, with management targeting 40% to 45% annual export growth as validation pipelines mature. That mix explains why Kross's revenue profile looks the way it does: truck and tractor forgings keep the Jamshedpur presses baseloaded with sticky OEM contracts, while complete trailer running-gear systems lift revenue per vehicle. The catch, which we trace in Chapter 3, is that system assemblies and raw-material backward integration consume far more working capital and fixed assets than simple machining.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: Sub-Component Vendor vs. System Supplier
paragraphs: Notice the strategic upgrade Kross has attempted since 2019: moving from a ₹2,000 forged shaft where the OEM owns the drawing to a ₹1,00,000+ trailer axle-and-suspension system where Kross owns the engineering assembly.
That shift raises ticket size and relevance, but it also forces the supplier to carry finished kits and finance trailer builders on longer credit terms.

book_subsections.title: Inside a 14-Tonne Trailer Axle Order
paragraphs: To make the segment mix concrete, picture a regional trailer bodybuilder in Raipur or Pune assembling a 40-foot flatbed semi-trailer for a steel and cement fleet. That builder has two choices for the three axles sitting underneath the trailer bed: buy cheaper welded-seam axles from an unorganized importer and risk weld fatigue on overloaded Indian highways, or buy single-piece extruded 13-tonne or 14-tonne axles from an organized supplier like Kross. Because Kross extrudes the axle beam from a single piece of alloy steel rather than welding three separate sections together, the beam eliminates the structural weld seam where cracks typically start under dynamic highway shock.

Roughly 80% of Kross’s trailer axle output now uses this single-piece extruded beam architecture, which is why trailer axles and suspensions climbed from roughly a third of revenue at the time of the IPO to 43%–49% of total sales by Q2 FY27. When that trailer builder orders a full tri-axle bogie kit—complete with forged hubs, brake drums, S-camshafts, and mechanical or air suspension—Kross captures far more revenue per trailer than it ever could by selling a loose forged shaft.

book_subsections.title: Why Precision Forgings Still Anchor the Factory Floor
paragraphs: Now walk across the aisle to the legacy forging and machining bays, which still generate slightly over half of Kross’s revenue. Here, the customer is not a fragmented trailer builder; it is an engineering team at Ashok Leyland, Tata Motors, or TAFE. Think about an axle shaft or a companion flange inside a 49-tonne tipper truck hauling iron ore out of a mine: if a forging fails under torque, the entire truck is stranded and the OEM faces warranty claims and safety recalls.

That safety-critical role explains why OEMs take two to three years to qualify a supplier’s heat-treatment and metallurgical controls before awarding a production program. It also explains why Kross’s European Tier-1 export push—currently about 8% of component revenue and targeted for ~45% growth in FY27—carries strategic weight beyond its current size. Every export SKU that passes European fatigue testing diversifies Kross away from domestic truck cycles, setting up the next question: how does Kross actually sell, finance, and deliver these parts?

What ties both segments together is metallurgical discipline: induction heating, controlled quench-and-temper cycles, and CNC finish machining under one Jamshedpur roof. That shared backbone lets Kross shift press hours between truck shafts and trailer hubs as demand ebbs and flows, though it also means capital intensity stays high across both engines.

Consider what that engineering shift means on an actual Indian highway. A loaded 55-tonne tractor-trailer running between Jamshedpur, Raipur, and Mumbai hits thousands of expansion joints and potholes every month. When an unorganized welded axle cracks at the center weld, the fleet owner loses days of freight revenue and faces roadside repair bills. Kross’s single-piece extruded beam removes that weld seam entirely, giving fleet operators a tangible reliability reason to pay for an organized Tier-1 assembly.

At the same time, keep the legacy forging business in clear view. Axle shafts, companion flanges, and tractor hydraulic lift parts still represent slightly over half of revenue and keep Kross embedded inside Ashok Leyland, Tata Motors, and TAFE assembly lines—giving the company both steady OEM volume and a bridge into European Tier-1 exports.

Every time you see a 14-tonne tri-axle trailer rolling down a national highway carrying steel coils or containers, remember the unit economics behind that vehicle. Selling an entire axle-and-suspension bogie instead of a single forged spindle multiplies Kross’s revenue per vehicle and deepens its engineering relevance to trailer builders.
Yet it also ties Kross’s growth rate directly to freight tonnage, infrastructure spending, and fleet financing cycles across India.

Together, the trailer-axle assembly division and the legacy forging bays form a tightly linked manufacturing ecosystem—one capturing higher system value per trailer, the other anchoring long-standing relationships with Tata Motors, Ashok Leyland, and TAFE.
